studies.title: From ancient guardian to modern spirit.
studies.summary: Yaksha needed more than a premium whisky identity. It needed a distinctive Indian point of view in a category crowded with familiar heritage codes. We built a brand world around the Yaksha guardian of hidden treasures translating mythology into a contemporary identity, packaging system, and ritual-led experience.

cardStats.label: Countries on one learning brand system

sections.title: The category was premium. The opportunity was cultural.
paragraphs: Premium whisky is filled with familiar visual codes: dark bottles, metallic finishes, heritage typography, crests, shields and stories borrowed from established whisky traditions.
Yaksha had an opportunity to take a different route.

Rather than imitate established premium whisky conventions, we looked at what India already had: a deep mythology filled with characters, rituals, symbols and stories that could create a world of its own.
The Yaksha, an ancient guardian associated with nature, abundance and hidden treasures, became the foundation.

sections.title: The opportunity was to create a whisky brand that felt
How do you make a new whisky brand impossible to ignore?
paragraphs: Yaksha needed to stand apart on shelf while creating enough depth to sustain an entire brand world beyond the bottle.

sections.label: The challenge in one line
sections.text: How do you turn an ancient Indian story into a contemporary premium identity that feels distinctive, desirable and scalable?

sections.title: From guardian to offering.
paragraphs: We reframed the role of the Yaksha.
The Yaksha is the **guardian**.
The whisky is the **treasure**.
The pour becomes the **offering**.
The experience becomes the **ritual**.
The idea gave us a simple strategic platform from which the identity, packaging and experience could all grow.

sections.title: Four pillars anchored every asset.
sections.intro: Long-term communication pillars gave hundreds of contributors a shared answer to 'what should this feel like?'

items.title: Art to the Science
items.desc: Learning is rigorous; the brand makes it beautiful. Every asset pairs instructional soundness with visual craft, never one without the other.

items.title: One Global Voice
items.desc: Confident, human, jargon-free. A tone litmus test shipped with the BrandBook: can a learner in any market understand it on first read?

items.title: Motion First
items.desc: Learning competes with everything else on an employee's screen. Motion, intros, transitions, kinetic type, earns the first five seconds.

items.title: Scale Without Sameness
items.desc: Templates flex by region and program tier, so assets feel local in language and global in identity, never photocopied.

sections.title: From audit to operating system.

items.title: Audit 300+ assets across regions.
items.desc: We collected three years of learning assets from every region and mapped the drift: 14 unofficial logo variants, 30+ color interpretations, no shared typography. The audit became the business case leadership presented internally.

items.title: Design the BrandBook.
items.desc: A complete visual language, lockups, color, typography, iconography, data-viz, photography and illustration codes, documented as a living BrandBook with do/don't examples pulled from the audit itself.

items.title: Ship templates, not rules.
items.desc: Slide systems, eLearning skins, video intro/outro packages, motion graphics kits, and program launch toolkits. Every rule in the BrandBook shipped with a matching asset a team could use in minutes.

items.title: Build the GenAI video pipeline.
items.desc: An AI-assisted pipeline turned approved scripts into on-brand animated explainers in days instead of months, with brand elements baked into the pipeline so speed never cost consistency.

sections.title: Ancient richness. Contemporary precision.
sections.intro: The identity was built around the tension between two worlds.
paragraphs: **Ancient × Modern**
**Ornate × Precise**
**Mystical × Contemporary**
Rich illustration and ornamentation create discovery and depth.
Clean typography and structured composition keep the brand contemporary.
The result is a visual language that feels culturally rooted without looking historical.

studies.title: Selling flats before the hoarding went up.
studies.summary: A mid-size developer with genuinely premium construction was being priced like everyone else, because their brand looked like everyone else. A full PRISM rebrand repositioned the project as the obvious premium choice in its micro-market, before a single hoarding went up.

sections.title: A premium product wearing a commodity costume.
paragraphs: The developer's build quality, amenities, and location genuinely beat the competing projects on the same stretch of highway. Buyers who visited the sample flat said so themselves.

But their brochure, site branding, and social presence looked identical to every other launch in the market: the same render-heavy hoardings, the same amenity checklists, the same shouting typography. Channel partners led every conversation with discounts. Buyers negotiated hard, because nothing signaled that this project deserved a premium.
The flagship residential tower launch was 10 weeks away. The brand had to change before the market formed its first impression, because in real estate, the first impression is the price anchor.

sections.title: Before defining the brand, we defined the buyer.
sections.intro: The core buyer for this project:
items: Upgrading from a 1–2 BHK within the same micro-market, they know every competing project
Researches on Instagram and property portals weeks before ever calling a number
Buys on trust signals: who else is buying, how the developer presents itself, how finished the details feel
Will pay a premium for certainty, but punishes anything that smells like over-promising
sections.outro: This buyer doesn't compare amenities line by line. They decide in seconds which project 'feels' more trustworthy, then rationalize with the checklist. That instinct is where the brand had to win.

sections.label: The challenge in one line
sections.text: How do you make a project command a premium per square foot, before construction is even visible from the road?

sections.title: Perceived value is designed, not discounted.
paragraphs: We audited 14 competing launches within the micro-market. Every single one shouted: exclamation-mark headlines, ten amenities per hoarding, gold-gradient everything. When everyone shouts, the confident whisper wins.
The strategy: own 'quiet luxury', the one position nobody in the market occupied. Craft over claims. Calm over noise. Long-term value over launch-weekend urgency.

Positioning the project this way did something subtle and powerful: it moved the buyer's comparison frame from 'price per square foot' to 'which of these will I be proud to live in?', a question our client won by default.

sections.title: Four codes of quiet luxury.

items.title: Craft Over Claims
items.desc: Show the shadow gap, the stone detail, the door hardware. Proof photographed beautifully beats adjectives printed loudly.

items.title: Calm Confidence
items.desc: Generous white space, restrained serif typography, one message per surface. The brand never raises its voice, because it doesn't need to.

items.title: Neighbourhood Pride
items.desc: Rooted in Vashi, not floating in render-land. Real streets, real light, real distances, the brand sells a life, not a skyline.

items.title: Proof in Detail
items.desc: Every touchpoint finishes like the building: aligned, considered, premium in the hand. The brochure paper stock is an argument for the flat.

sections.title: Eight weeks, one system.

items.title: Map the market, claim the gap.
items.desc: Competitor audit of 14 launches, buyer interviews at competing sample flats, channel-partner conversations. Output: a positioning statement the sales team could recite, and price against.

items.title: Design an identity that raises the price.
items.desc: A restrained serif wordmark, architectural photography direction, an editorial layout system, and a materials palette, designed to feel like a property magazine, not a pamphlet.

items.title: Build every buyer touchpoint as one kit.
items.desc: Brochure, walkthrough film, hoarding and site signage, sample-flat wayfinding, channel-partner kit, landing page, and WhatsApp collateral, one consistent system handed to sales on day one.

items.title: Launch the waitlist before the hoarding.
items.desc: A teaser campaign across Instagram and channel partners drove site-visit bookings from a waitlist before public launch, letting sales anchor pricing high from the first conversation.

sections.title: The parts of quiet luxury.

items.name: Wordmark & Monogram
items.desc: A high-contrast serif wordmark with a drawn monogram for signage and embossing, engineered to look expensive at hoarding scale and letterhead scale alike.

items.name: Colour Palette
items.desc: Deep indigo, warm ivory, and stone grey, with a single metallic accent reserved for print finishing, restraint as a status signal.

items.name: Typography
items.desc: An editorial serif for headlines and a quiet grotesque for information, the pairing of a magazine, not a mass mailer.

items.name: Photography Direction
items.desc: Natural light, human scale, material close-ups. No fish-eye renders, no saturated skies, believability is the luxury.

items.name: Layout System
items.desc: A strict editorial grid across brochure, hoarding, and web: one image, one line, one message per surface.

items.name: Signage & Environment
items.desc: Site hoarding, sample-flat wayfinding, and sales-lounge graphics that carry the same calm through the physical journey.

studies.title: The product was great. The listing was killing it.
studies.summary: A fast-growing Ayurvedic wellness brand had a product customers loved and listings that buried it. We rebuilt the packaging, listing imagery, and A+ content as one conversion system, and let the numbers do the talking.

cardStats.label: Return on ad spend, same budget

sections.title: Traffic without trust.
paragraphs: The founders had built something real: honest formulations, loyal repeat customers, five-star reviews from everyone who actually tried the product. Growth capital was going into ads, and the ads were working, clicks were cheap and plentiful.

Then the clicks landed on the listing. Inconsistent packshots. Text-heavy infographics unreadable on a phone. Packaging that disappeared next to bigger competitors on the search results page. Conversion sat well below category benchmarks, which meant every rupee of ad spend was working twice as hard as it should.
The founders were about to cut ad budgets. The real problem was the brand at the point of decision.

sections.title: We audited the category shelf first.
paragraphs: Before touching a pixel, we screenshotted the top 30 competing listings across marketplaces and mapped their visual codes: what colors dominate the search page, what claims lead, what the thumbnail war actually looks like at 2 inches wide.

The pattern: everyone decorates, nobody proves. Leaf motifs, gold flourishes, Sanskrit typography, and claims floating without evidence. The gap was a brand that looks calm and clinical-adjacent: proof-forward, legible at thumbnail size, honest in tone.
That audit became the design brief. We would win the thumbnail with clarity, and win the cart with proof.

sections.label: The challenge in one line
sections.text: How do you turn a 2-inch thumbnail on a crowded search page into the most trustworthy thing a buyer sees that day?

sections.title: Win the thumbnail, win the cart.
paragraphs: Ecommerce branding isn't brand-book branding. The 'logo on a mood board' matters less than the exact sequence of images a thumb scrolls through between doubt and checkout.

So we treated the listing itself as the brand's flagship store: seven frames per SKU, each with one job, hook, proof, ritual, ingredients, comparison, social proof, promise. The packaging was redesigned to serve frame one; the A+ content was designed to close frame seven.
One system, engineered around a single behavioural truth: buyers don't read listings, they scroll them. Every frame had to work alone, in order, on a phone.

sections.title: Seven frames, one job each.
sections.intro: Every SKU shipped with the same conversion sequence, customized in content, identical in logic.

items.title: Frame 1, The Hook
items.desc: Pack-forward hero with the single strongest claim. Designed to be legible and differentiated at thumbnail size in search results.

items.title: Frames 2–3, The Proof
items.desc: Clinical-adjacent evidence: ingredient percentages, sourcing, certifications, designed like lab notes, not decoration.

items.title: Frames 4–5, The Ritual
items.desc: How it fits a real morning: dosage, timing, taste. Lifestyle photography that looks like the buyer's own kitchen, not a stock resort.

items.title: Frames 6–7, The Close
items.desc: Review wall with real customer language, then the promise frame: guarantee, delivery, and the reorder ritual.

sections.title: Six weeks from audit to relaunch.

items.title: Category shelf audit.
items.desc: Top 30 listings mapped for visual codes, claim hierarchies, and thumbnail legibility. Deliberately designed against the category: calm where they shout, proof where they decorate.

items.title: Packaging built for a 2-inch thumbnail.
items.desc: Refreshed pack architecture with a bold ingredient mark and high-contrast hierarchy, the pack itself became the best-performing pixel in the hero frame.

items.title: The 7-frame listing system.
items.desc: Photography direction, infographic templates, A+ content modules, and a brand storefront, one system applied across 12 SKUs so the whole catalog converts consistently.

items.title: Test, read, iterate.
items.desc: A/B tests on hero frames and claim order across two hero SKUs. Winning variants rolled out catalog-wide and repurposed into ad creative, closing the loop between listing and ads.

studies.title: From referred CA to the obvious choice.
studies.summary: A senior CA advising funded startups relied entirely on word of mouth, invisible to founders searching for exactly what he offered. The PRISM Method rebuilt his positioning, identity, and content system so credibility compounded in public, not just in referrals.

sections.title: Fifteen years of expertise the market never saw.
paragraphs: A client roster of funded startups. War stories from due-diligence rooms. The kind of finance instincts founders pay premium retainers for, once they find him. The problem was that they never found him.

His LinkedIn read like a resume from 2014. His website was a contact form. Founders picked flashier advisors with weaker credentials, because those advisors looked authoritative online, and every engagement he did win started with a discount conversation, because nothing in his presence signaled premium.
He didn't need more competence. He needed a brand that matched it.

sections.title: The founder who needed to find him.
sections.intro: We profiled the exact person the brand had to reach:
items: Founder of a funded D2C or SaaS startup, ₹2–50 Cr revenue, drowning in finance decisions
Lives on LinkedIn and founder WhatsApp groups, that's where advisors get discovered and vetted
Judges expertise by public thinking: frameworks, teardowns, and specific numbers, not certificates
Ready to pay premium for an advisor who has visibly 'seen this movie before'
sections.outro: This audience never opens a directory of CAs. They follow three or four finance voices, and when the pain arrives, they message the one they already trust. The brand's job: become that voice.

sections.label: The challenge in one line
sections.text: How does a quiet expert become the finance voice founders already trust, before they ever need to search for one?

sections.title: Authority is a system, not a flex.
paragraphs: Personal branding for professionals usually fails in one of two ways: it stays a resume (credible but invisible), or it becomes influencer cosplay (visible but not credible). The strategy had to hold both: unmistakable expertise, published consistently.
The PRISM move was narrowing: from 'CA for everyone' to 'the finance brain for funded D2C startups.' A narrower promise reads as deeper expertise, and deeper expertise commands wider margins.
Then we made publishing sustainable. A senior advisor doesn't have four hours a day for content. The system had to turn one hour a week into a compounding public body of work.

sections.title: Four content pillars he can actually sustain.

items.title: Frameworks
items.desc: Named, repeatable finance frameworks for D2C founders, the shareable assets that turn one post into a referral engine.

items.title: War Stories
items.desc: Anonymized lessons from real due-diligence and fundraise rooms. Specificity founders can't get from generic finance content.

items.title: Founder Finance Rituals
items.desc: The weekly numbers habit: what to review, when, and what it prevents. Practical enough to screenshot and pin.

items.title: Contrarian POV
items.desc: Respectful heresy on funding, valuation, and growth-at-all-costs, the posts that make founders argue in the comments and follow for more.

sections.title: Ten weeks on the PRISM Method.

items.title: Niche down to the profitable edge.
items.desc: Positioning workshops, client interviews, and competitor voice mapping. Output: a one-line promise, 'the finance brain for funded D2C startups', and the proof points to defend it.

items.title: A personal identity, not a corporate costume.
items.desc: Monogram, typography, and a signature visual style for frameworks and carousels, professional enough for boardrooms, distinctive enough to be recognized mid-scroll.

items.title: A content engine that runs on one hour a week.
items.desc: LinkedIn profile overhaul, 90-day calendar, carousel and framework templates, and a one-page site with a single conversion goal: book the advisory call.

items.title: Publish, measure, compound.
items.desc: Weekly cadence with monthly reviews. Winning posts became lead magnets; lead magnets became advisory calls; calls became retainers, the compounding loop personal brands are supposed to be.

sections.title: The personal brand kit.

items.name: Monogram & Wordmark
items.desc: A drawn monogram that works as a LinkedIn avatar at 40px and on a letterhead at full size, one mark for every context an advisor lives in.

items.name: Colour & Typography
items.desc: A deep navy base with a restrained accent, serious without being sombre. An editorial serif for authority, a clean grotesque for frameworks and data.

items.name: Carousel & Framework Templates
items.desc: A recognizable visual grammar for weekly frameworks: consistent grids, chart styles, and cover typography that reads as 'his' before the name appears.

items.name: Profile & Site
items.desc: LinkedIn overhaul, banner, headline, featured section, plus a one-page site with a single call to action: book the advisory call.

items.name: Speaker Kit
items.desc: A one-pager and slide template for podcasts and panels, so every appearance feeds the same brand instead of diluting it.
